messages.content: I want to build a loop vectorizer that preserves scalar semantics even when a loop has data-dependent exits, accesses that may alias, and loads that can fault. The requirements are to preserve observable write ordering and precise faults without accessing memory beyond the scalar exit, while achieving 1.3× throughput versus optimized scalar code on three representative loops combining exits and aliasing.

That sets two distinct requirements: semantic equivalence to scalar execution and a throughput target. The vectorized loop must preserve the observable order of writes and the fault behavior of the scalar loop. In particular, it must not access memory that scalar execution would leave untouched because it exited. Separately, the target is 1.3× the throughput of optimized scalar code on three representative loops combining exits and aliasing. That is a goal, not a reported result.
Why does a data-dependent exit make the memory condition especially important?

The point where scalar execution stops depends on data encountered while the loop runs. A vectorized form may consider several iterations together, but doing so cannot justify a memory access from an iteration the scalar loop would never reach. Even if the result of that access were discarded, the access itself could be observable—for example, if it faults.
So producing the same final values would not be enough?

Right. Matching final values does not by itself preserve observable write ordering or precise faults, and it does not establish that no memory was accessed beyond the scalar exit. Those are explicit parts of the required scalar semantics.
How should I read “precise faults” here?

Fault behavior must correspond to scalar execution, rather than to an access performed merely because work was grouped into a vector. If the scalar loop would exit before reaching a load, a fault from that load would not be faithful to scalar semantics. Conversely, vectorization cannot simply ignore a fault from a load the scalar execution does reach.
And potentially aliasing accesses affect the write-order requirement?

Yes. When accesses may refer to the same memory location, their order can affect what is observed. Preserving observable write ordering means the vectorized execution cannot assume such accesses are independent and freely change the effects that scalar execution would expose.
Does that mean the vectorizer cannot reorganize anything?

Not necessarily. The requirement is about preserving scalar semantics, not preserving every internal step in the same form. Any reorganization would have to maintain the observable order of writes, precise faults, and the boundary set by the scalar exit. The goal does not prescribe a particular implementation technique.
I also want to be careful about what the 1.3× figure claims.

It is a throughput target relative to optimized scalar code, not a claim that the vectorizer has already reached it. The stated comparison is specifically on three representative loops combining exits and aliasing; it does not, by itself, assert the same throughput across all loops.
Are the correctness conditions limited to those three loops?

The goal is to build a vectorizer preserving scalar semantics across data-dependent exits, potentially aliasing accesses, and faulting loads. The three representative loops identify where the 1.3× throughput target is to be assessed. They do not narrow the stated semantic requirements to a performance measurement alone.
Would it be accurate to describe the exit boundary as more than just a question of which results get kept?

Yes. The boundary constrains which memory accesses may occur at all. Discarding a value from an iteration beyond the scalar exit would not undo an access already made there, nor would it undo a fault from that access.
What if an access beyond the exit happens not to fault?

The requirement still says not to access memory beyond the scalar exit. Faulting loads make the risk especially clear, but the no-access condition is not conditional on whether a particular access faults.
I think the hard part is that these constraints have to hold together rather than one at a time.

That is a fair reading of the goal. A vectorized execution must respect the data-dependent stopping point, preserve observable write ordering despite potential aliasing, and keep faults precise. Meeting one of those conditions does not excuse violating another, and the 1.3× throughput target remains a separate requirement against optimized scalar code on the three representative loops.

For that vectorizer, I’m proposing a guarded chunk approach: guard chunk dereferenceability and disjointness, scan exits sequentially, mask live-lane loads, and commit stores in order. Otherwise, fall back to scalar execution.

That proposal separates permission to use a chunk from the work done within it. The dereferenceability and disjointness guards address whether the chunk can safely use the guarded path. The sequential exit scan determines how far scalar execution would proceed; loads are then limited to live lanes, and stores are committed in order. If the guarded path’s conditions are not met, the proposed alternative is scalar execution.
What is the dereferenceability guard meant to establish? I don’t want it mistaken for permission to load every lane.

Those are different points. Guarding chunk dereferenceability is a condition for taking the guarded path, but it does not override the scalar exit. The live-lane mask still has to prevent loads from iterations whose memory accesses scalar execution would not reach. Establishing that an address could be dereferenced is not the same as being permitted to dereference it in this execution.
And the guard itself should not violate the exit rule, right?

Right. The requirement not to access memory beyond the scalar exit applies to the whole execution, including whatever is done to decide whether to use the guarded path. A guard cannot preserve precise faults if evaluating it performs an out-of-bounds-of-scalar-execution memory access. The proposal does not specify how the guard is implemented, so that remains a constraint on any implementation of it.
Why scan exits sequentially if the rest of the chunk is vectorized?

Because the exit is data-dependent, the scalar stopping point must be respected before treating later lanes as live. A sequential scan preserves the order in which exit decisions matter to scalar execution. Vectorizing other work within a chunk does not make an iteration after the scalar exit eligible for a memory access.
Does “live lane” simply mean every lane before the first exit?

It means a lane whose particular operation would be reached under scalar semantics. The proposal does not define where a load falls relative to an exit decision within an iteration, so a blanket rule about the exiting iteration would be too strong. The load mask must reflect which loads scalar execution would actually perform.
Suppose the mask excludes a lane, but a load still happens and its result is ignored. Would that count?

No. Masking live-lane loads has to constrain the memory accesses themselves, not merely which results are retained. A load from an inactive lane could fault, and an access beyond the scalar exit would violate the stated requirement even if it did not fault.
What role does disjointness play alongside ordered stores?

The disjointness guard addresses the possibility that accesses in the chunk alias. Ordered store commits address the observable order of writes. They serve different purposes: a disjointness condition cannot replace the requirement to commit stores in order, and ordered commits do not by themselves establish that other accesses can safely be treated as disjoint.
If disjointness cannot be established, am I proposing to proceed more cautiously within the vector path?
As stated, the proposal says to fall back to scalar execution otherwise. It does not specify an additional vector path for a chunk whose disjointness guard is not satisfied.
I want “commit ordered stores” to be understood as preserving observable behavior, not just issuing a batch of writes eventually.

Yes. The point of ordered commits is to preserve the order of writes that scalar execution makes observable. That includes avoiding writes from iterations beyond the scalar exit; merely producing the same eventual memory contents would not necessarily preserve the required ordering.
Could the fallback be read as a correctness escape hatch rather than a claim that scalar code is fast?

Yes. Falling back to scalar execution is the proposed behavior when the guarded chunk path cannot be used. It speaks to preserving scalar semantics under those conditions; it is not evidence that the separate 1.3× throughput target versus optimized scalar code has been reached on the three representative loops.
So this is still a design proposal, not a demonstrated solution?

Correct. The proposed combination is chunk dereferenceability and disjointness guards, a sequential exit scan, live-lane-masked loads, ordered store commits, and scalar fallback otherwise. Whether an implementation satisfies precise faults, avoids all memory access beyond the scalar exit, preserves observable write ordering, and reaches the stated throughput target would still have to be established.
There’s an ordering question in the chunk proposal: when a store aliases a later exit-predicate load, can exit scanning precede ordered stores without changing the exit lane?

Not unconditionally. In scalar order, the store happens before that later predicate load. If the store changes the value the load observes, scanning the exit first could test an earlier value and identify a different exit lane. Committing the stores in order afterward would not repair an exit decision already made from that earlier value.
So scanning exit decisions sequentially is not, by itself, enough to preserve scalar order?

Right. Sequential scanning preserves the order among the exit tests, but it does not place an earlier store before a later test if all the tests are scanned before stores are committed. The relevant ordering is between the store and the predicate load, not only between one predicate load and the next.
Could you give a simple conceptual example without assuming anything about the actual loops?

Imagine an earlier iteration stores a value that makes a later iteration’s exit condition true. Scalar execution performs the store, then the later predicate load sees that value and exits. If a prescan reads the predicate before the store takes effect, it might find the condition false and choose a later exit lane. That is only an illustration of the dependency; it does not assert that any particular loop has it.
Would the disjointness guard in the proposal answer the question?

It could answer it for a guarded chunk if the guard actually establishes that the stores cannot alias the later exit-predicate loads whose ordering would otherwise matter. Merely having a guard called “disjointness” is not enough to infer its coverage. If the store and predicate load may alias on the path being taken, the proposed scan-before-commit ordering still needs justification.
What if they alias but the store happens to write the value that was already there?

Then that particular predicate load might observe the same value either way. But the fact that this can happen in a particular case does not make prescanning safe whenever aliasing is possible. The question is whether the exit decision is guaranteed to match scalar execution for the cases in which that path runs.
Is this only a problem when the changed value makes the loop exit earlier?

No. A changed predicate value could move the selected exit lane in either direction, depending on the predicate and value. The essential issue is that reading before an earlier scalar-order store can change the decision. Either kind of change would matter to which later memory accesses and writes scalar execution reaches.
Suppose I keep the stores ordered relative to each other, but do the exit scan before any of them. What exactly is still missing?

Store-to-store order would be preserved, but the earlier store would still be ordered after a predicate load that scalar execution performs later. If that load aliases the store, the scan might observe the wrong value. Ordered commits address the order among committed writes; they do not automatically preserve the order of a write relative to a dependent exit-predicate load.
And a wrong exit lane feeds back into the live-lane mask?

Yes. The exit lane determines which operations are live under the proposed scheme. If the scan chooses a lane different from scalar execution’s, the load mask could admit an access scalar execution would not make, or omit one it would make. That connects this ordering question directly to the requirements on memory access and precise faults.
Can we answer the original question as a conditional, then, rather than saying the approach always works or never works?

Yes. Exit scanning can precede ordered stores without changing the exit lane only if the predicate loads used by that scan are guaranteed to produce the scalar-order exit decisions despite those stores not yet being committed. A disjointness guarantee covering the relevant store–predicate-load pairs is one way the dependency could be absent. Where such a dependency remains possible, scanning first cannot simply be assumed to preserve the exit lane.
Does the scalar fallback settle the case where that guarantee cannot be established?

Under the stated proposal, the guarded path is used only when its conditions hold; otherwise execution falls back to scalar. That makes it important to know whether the condition for taking the guarded path covers this store-to-exit-predicate-load dependency. The question alone does not establish that it does, or that any implementation has been tested.

I have a hypothesis about the ordering question: an earlier store that aliases a later exit-predicate load invalidates a precommit exit scan. A cross-lane overlap guard, with scalar fallback when it detects that overlap, should preserve the exit lane.

The dependency is the key point. Scalar execution performs the earlier store before the later predicate load. A precommit scan reverses that relationship: it can read the predicate before the store takes effect and therefore choose a different exit lane. Under your hypothesis, the guarded path excludes that cross-lane overlap, while the overlapping case uses scalar execution and retains scalar ordering.
Does “invalidates” mean that every such overlap definitely changes the exit lane?

No. An overlap does not prove that the predicate value or exit lane changes in every execution. It means the precommit scan cannot generally rely on seeing the value that scalar execution would see. The guard treats the possible dependency as a reason not to use that scan-first path.
Why specify an earlier store and a later predicate load, rather than just saying that stores and loads must not overlap?

Because the proposed failure mode has a direction in scalar order. The load belongs to a later lane and should observe the effects of an earlier lane’s store if their accesses overlap. Scanning that load before committing the store can break that ordering. The hypothesis is specifically about detecting that cross-lane store-to-predicate-load relationship.
So the guard has to cover the predicate loads used to choose the exit lane, not merely the stores?

Yes. For the stated hypothesis to preserve exit lanes, its overlap check must cover the relevant earlier stores and later exit-predicate loads. A check that misses one of those pairs would leave the scan-first path exposed to the same ordering issue.
If overlap is detected, why does scalar fallback help?

Scalar execution retains the order at issue: it performs an earlier store before reaching a later predicate load. Falling back in the overlapping case avoids choosing an exit lane from a predicate value read before that store. This explains the proposed exit-lane protection; it is not a report that a guard or fallback has already been implemented or verified.
What should happen when the guard finds no such cross-lane overlap?

On this hypothesis, the particular earlier-store-to-later-predicate-load dependency is absent from the guarded chunk. That removes this reason for a precommit scan to choose a different exit lane. It does not, on its own, establish every other requirement of the vectorizer.
Would ordered store commits alone solve this dependency?

No. Committing stores in their scalar order relative to one another does not make a predicate load performed during an earlier scan observe a store that has not yet been committed. The overlap guard and fallback address whether that scan-first ordering can be used at all for the relevant lanes.
Could the guard itself read the later predicate values to decide whether overlap matters?

That would need care. The guard is meant to prevent an unsafe predicate read from being justified by the guarded path; it cannot assume permission to perform memory accesses beyond the scalar exit merely to decide whether to take that path. Your hypothesis identifies what overlap must be excluded, but it does not specify how the guard determines overlap.
I want to keep the claim appropriately narrow. What exactly is the proposed guarantee?

It is a hypothesis about preserving exit lanes: exclude cross-lane overlap between earlier stores and later exit-predicate loads from the precommit-scan path, and use scalar fallback when that overlap is present. The claim does not by itself demonstrate precise faults, the absence of all memory access beyond the scalar exit, observable write ordering in every other case, or the 1.3× throughput target.
And if a store aliases a later predicate load but happens not to affect that predicate in one instance?

The guard can still route that instance to scalar execution. The hypothesis does not depend on proving that each individual overlap changes the result; it uses the overlap to identify a case in which the precommit scan cannot generally be assumed to reproduce the scalar exit lane.

I want to turn the overlap hypothesis into an implementation and validation plan: implement cross-lane predicate/store overlap checks, sequential exit scans, and scalar fallback. Then validate fault addresses and store traces against scalar execution.

That keeps the ordering question central. The overlap checks address whether an earlier lane’s store could affect a later lane’s exit-predicate load. Sequential exit scans retain the order of the exit decisions on the guarded path, and scalar fallback handles cases that cannot take that path. Comparing fault addresses and store traces with scalar execution would test observable consequences rather than only comparing final values.
For the overlap check, which direction of dependence matters here?

The relevant direction is an earlier store followed, in scalar execution, by a later exit-predicate load. If they overlap, scanning the predicate before committing that store may read a value different from the one scalar execution would read. The planned check needs to account for that cross-lane relationship; simply checking that two operations are in different lanes would not resolve it.
Does the sequential scan make the overlap check unnecessary?

No. A sequential scan orders the predicate evaluations relative to each other. It does not, by itself, place an earlier store before a later predicate load if stores have not yet been committed. The overlap check addresses that distinct store-to-predicate dependency.
And scalar fallback is part of the plan, not something to describe as already working?

Correct. The plan is to implement scalar fallback for cases that cannot use the guarded path. It has not yet established that the overlap checks correctly identify those cases or that the fallback is invoked under all the necessary conditions.
Why compare fault addresses instead of merely checking whether both executions fault?

Two executions can both fault yet do so at different memory accesses. Comparing fault addresses with scalar execution gives a more specific check on precise fault behavior. It is still validation to perform, not evidence already obtained.
What should “store traces” convey in that comparison?

A store trace can capture the observable sequence of writes for comparison with scalar execution. That matters because equal final memory contents would not necessarily show that writes occurred in scalar order or that no extra write occurred before an exit or fault. The plan names store-trace comparison; it does not yet report what any comparison shows.
Could matching store traces alone establish that no load accessed memory beyond the scalar exit?

No. A load might occur without producing a store, so a matching store trace would not by itself rule out an extra load. Fault-address comparison can expose some incorrect accesses when they fault, but the broader requirement not to access memory beyond the scalar exit remains a correctness condition on the implementation.
Should I treat the overlap check as proof that every other memory issue is handled?

No. It targets the particular risk that an earlier store changes what a later exit-predicate load should observe. The existing requirements concerning precise faults, live-lane memory access, and observable write order still apply. The plan’s validation comparisons can examine important effects, but the overlap check alone is not a general proof of them.
I’m trying to keep the sequence clear: the overlap check decides whether the scan-first path is appropriate, and the exit scan decides which lanes are live. Is that fair?

As a description of the proposed roles, yes. The overlap check is meant to exclude the store-to-later-predicate-load dependency from the scan-first path. The sequential scan then determines exit behavior for a path that is allowed to use it; otherwise the plan calls for scalar fallback. Neither role should be taken as permission to access memory beyond the scalar exit.
When we compare against scalar, what does the scalar run represent?

It is the reference for the semantics the vectorizer must preserve. Fault addresses can be compared against the faulting scalar execution, and store traces can be compared against the scalar sequence of writes. The point is to check the planned implementation against scalar behavior, not to treat a vectorized outcome as its own reference.
Does this plan say anything about whether we have achieved the throughput target?

No. Implementing the checks, scans, and fallback, and validating fault addresses and store traces, are planned work. The goal still includes 1.3× throughput versus optimized scalar code on three representative loops combining exits and aliasing, but this plan supplies no measured throughput or conclusion about meeting that target.
Then the immediate claim is only that we have a concrete way to investigate the dependency and its observable effects?

Yes. The plan specifies what to implement—cross-lane predicate/store overlap checks, sequential exit scans, and scalar fallback—and what to compare with scalar execution: fault addresses and store traces. Those comparisons are intended to assess whether the implemented behavior preserves the relevant scalar observations; their results are not yet known.
The next activity is to run ExitAlias-12 differential tests with cross-lane predicate/store overlaps and guard pages. I want to compare fallback decisions, exits, store traces, and faults.

That focuses the tests on the dependency the overlap guard is meant to handle. ExitAlias-12 can exercise cases where an earlier lane’s store overlaps a later lane’s exit-predicate load, while guard pages make an unintended memory access easier to detect through a fault. The differential comparisons should keep two questions distinct: whether the guarded path or scalar fallback was selected appropriately, and whether execution’s exits, store traces, and faults match scalar behavior.
Why compare fallback decisions separately from the exit results?

Because a matching exit in one case would not establish that the overlap guard selected the intended path. The fallback decision tells you whether a detected cross-lane predicate/store overlap was routed away from the precommit-scan path. The exit comparison asks whether the resulting execution stopped where scalar execution stopped. They examine different parts of the proposed approach.
Scalar execution doesn’t make a fallback decision, though. What is that decision compared with?

The fallback decision is assessed against the guard condition and the intended handling of the overlap, not against a decision made by scalar execution. Scalar execution supplies the reference for observable behavior: the exit, store trace, and fault. Keeping those comparisons separate avoids implying that the scalar reference has a vector-path decision.
What does an exit comparison tell us that a store-trace comparison might miss?

It directly checks the chosen stopping point. Two executions might produce the same recorded writes in a particular case yet disagree about which lane caused the exit. That disagreement would still matter, especially because the exit determines which later memory accesses are permitted.
And why retain the store traces if we already compare exits?

Matching the exit does not establish that writes occurred in the scalar-observable order. Comparing store traces checks for differences in the sequence of writes, including writes that should not occur before the scalar exit. It addresses an observable requirement that the exit comparison alone cannot settle.
How do guard pages contribute to the fault comparison?

They provide a way for an otherwise unintended access to manifest as a fault. In these tests, a fault comparison can reveal whether execution reaches an address that scalar execution would not, or disagrees with scalar execution about a fault it should encounter. Guard pages are a testing aid; their presence does not make accesses beyond the scalar exit permissible when those accesses happen not to fault.
Should “compare faults” include where the fault occurs, rather than just whether there is one?

Yes. Comparing the faulting address, where there is a fault, is important to the precise-fault requirement. Merely observing that both executions fault would not show that they faulted on the same scalar-reachable access. The activity calls for comparing faults; no outcome of that comparison is stated yet.
If an overlapping case takes scalar fallback and matches the scalar exit, what would that establish?

For that tested case, it would show the observed fallback choice and exit agree with the intended handling and scalar reference, respectively. The store trace and fault comparison would still be needed for the other observations. One matching case would not establish that every overlap is detected or that every execution preserves scalar semantics.
Could a non-faulting access beyond the exit escape these comparisons?

It could escape detection from fault and store comparisons alone: a load might neither fault nor produce a write. The requirement remains to avoid accessing memory beyond the scalar exit altogether. ExitAlias-12 differential observations can test important consequences of a violation, but a passing comparison would need to be interpreted within what was actually observed.
The cross-lane overlap cases are specifically about the store affecting a later exit-predicate load, correct?

Yes. That is the dependency under examination: scalar execution places the earlier store before the later predicate load, whereas a precommit exit scan could read the predicate first. The fallback-decision and exit comparisons are particularly relevant to whether the guard handles that ordering risk.
I don’t want to describe the tests as having confirmed the hypothesis before they run.

Then describe ExitAlias-12 as the differential testing activity, not as a result. The activity is to run the cases with cross-lane predicate/store overlaps and guard pages, and compare fallback decisions, exits, store traces, and faults. Whether those comparisons support the proposed guard-and-fallback behavior remains to be seen.
Does this activity measure the 1.3× throughput target?

Not as stated. ExitAlias-12 is described here as differential testing of fallback decisions and scalar-observable behavior. It supplies no throughput measurements against optimized scalar code on the three representative loops, so no performance conclusion follows from this activity alone.
So even if the exit lane agrees, we should still inspect the other comparisons?

Yes. A matching exit is only one part of the differential check. The fallback decision addresses whether the overlap was handled through the intended path, the store trace addresses observable write order, and the fault comparison addresses precise fault behavior. None of those should be inferred solely from an exit-lane match.
ExitAlias-12 found 2/12 wrong exit lanes. The range-based overlap guards missed indexed stores that aliased later exit-predicate loads.

That is a concrete failure of exit-lane preservation in two of the twelve ExitAlias-12 cases. The reported cause is specific: the range-based guards did not catch indexed stores overlapping later predicate loads. Those cases could therefore reach an exit decision without the relevant earlier store-to-later-load relationship being accounted for.
Is it fair to say the sequential exit scan did not protect those two cases?

Yes, in the limited sense shown by the result. Scanning predicates sequentially does not restore scalar ordering between an earlier store and a later predicate load if that store has not taken effect. The two wrong exit lanes show that the tested combination did not preserve the scalar exit decision in those cases.
Does the 2/12 figure mean the other ten cases passed every differential comparison?

No. It reports two wrong exit lanes out of twelve cases. It does not state the outcomes for fallback decisions, store traces, or faults, or establish that every other property passed in the remaining cases.
I want to be precise about what the guard missed. Was it aliasing in general?

The finding is narrower: range-based overlap guards missed indexed stores aliasing later exit-predicate loads. It does not say that every kind of alias escaped detection, nor that every indexed store causes a wrong exit lane.
How does the indexed store matter to the earlier ordering question?

The ordering issue arises when scalar execution performs that store before a later predicate load that accesses overlapping memory. If the guard misses the overlap, a precommit scan may evaluate the later predicate without the earlier store’s effect. The observed wrong exit lanes show that this possibility mattered in two tested cases.
Can I conclude the scalar fallback itself was wrong?

Not from this finding. It identifies misses by the range-based overlap guards, not a defect in scalar execution. The reported result does not provide enough detail about fallback decisions in those cases to make a separate claim about the fallback’s implementation.
What does this say about using range-based guards to establish disjointness for the scan?

As tested in ExitAlias-12, those guards did not establish the needed lack of overlap for all relevant predicate/store pairs. The indexed-store aliases they missed undermine relying on the guard to justify scanning those later predicates before the earlier stores. That conclusion concerns the reported cases and guard behavior, rather than every conceivable range-based check.
Is a wrong exit lane just a bookkeeping error if stores eventually commit in order?

No. Ordered store commits cannot retroactively correct an exit decision made from the wrong predicate observation. The exit lane determines how far scalar execution proceeds, so a wrong lane is itself a semantic discrepancy and may affect which operations are treated as live. The result does not, however, specify what store traces or faults actually showed.
Would it be accurate to report that ExitAlias-12 found a fault mismatch too?

No. The stated result reports 2/12 wrong exit lanes and attributes them to range-based guards missing indexed-store aliases with later predicate loads. Although fault comparison was part of the test activity, no fault outcome is given here.
So the evidence is about an actual observed exit mismatch, not merely a theoretical concern about aliasing?

Exactly. The ordering concern is manifested in the reported result: two of twelve cases had wrong exit lanes, with the guard miss identified as the cause. That supports a concrete conclusion about those tested exit decisions without supplying results for the other differential comparisons or the throughput target.

My revised hypothesis is that a precommit exit scan requires dereference-free, exact-address proofs that include indexed stores and exclude overlap between an earlier store and a later exit-predicate load. If those proofs cannot be made, execution should fall back to scalar.

That makes the condition for scanning before store commits more specific. The guarded path would need to establish, for the relevant chunk, that each earlier store and later exit-predicate load cannot access the same address—even when the store is indexed. If it cannot establish that without dereferencing memory, the hypothesis calls for scalar fallback rather than a precommit scan.
Why insist on exact addresses instead of a broader description of the accesses?

The proposed proof has to settle the particular overlap that could change an exit decision. An approximate description that leaves an indexed store’s actual address unresolved cannot establish that the store is disjoint from a later predicate load. “Exact-address” here describes the precision needed for the proposed decision; it does not assert that such addresses are always available.
Does the proof have to show that every memory access in the chunk is disjoint from every other one?

Not as this hypothesis is stated. Its specific condition is to exclude earlier-store/later-predicate-load overlaps that would undermine a precommit exit scan. Other semantic requirements still apply, but this hypothesis should not be broadened into a claim that proving those particular pairs disjoint proves all accesses independent.
What does “including indexed stores” add to the condition?

It prevents the overlap decision from considering only addresses that a simpler range description happens to cover. An indexed store’s address must be accounted for in the exact-address proof when checking it against later exit-predicate loads. If that address cannot be established sufficiently for the check, this hypothesis sends execution to scalar fallback.
I’m also concerned that checking addresses could itself cause a forbidden access. Is that what “dereference-free” addresses?

Yes. The proposed proof must not perform a memory dereference merely to decide whether a precommit scan is safe. In particular, it cannot justify reading memory beyond the scalar exit as part of establishing permission to use the guarded path. If establishing the needed addresses would require such a dereference, the stated alternative is scalar execution.
Is determining an address the same thing as loading from that address?

No. An address may be determined without accessing the memory it names. The distinction matters here because the hypothesis calls for an exact-address proof that is dereference-free: it concerns identifying potential overlap without performing the predicate load or store access as part of the proof. Whether that can be done in a particular case is not established by the hypothesis.
Suppose the proof cannot decide whether one earlier store overlaps one later predicate load. May the scan go ahead because the overlap is only possible?

Not under this hypothesis. The precommit scan requires a proof excluding the relevant overlap. An unresolved possibility does not meet that condition, so the proposed behavior is scalar fallback. That is a condition for choosing the path, not a claim that every possible overlap actually changes the exit lane.
And if an exact-address check shows an overlap, does it matter whether the stored value would change the predicate?

The hypothesis does not rely on determining that value’s effect. An earlier-store/later-predicate overlap fails the exclusion needed for a precommit scan, and the stated response is scalar fallback. It avoids assuming that scanning the predicate before the store would happen to produce the same decision.
How does this answer the question of whether scanning can precede ordered stores?

It gives a conditional answer: the proposed precommit scan is allowed only when a dereference-free, exact-address proof excludes the relevant earlier-store/later-predicate overlaps, including those involving indexed stores. Otherwise, scalar execution preserves the store-before-predicate ordering at issue. This is a hypothesis about how to protect exit decisions, not a demonstrated guarantee.
Would a sequential scan by itself satisfy that condition?

No. Sequentially evaluating exit predicates preserves their order relative to one another, but it does not make a predicate load observe an earlier store that has not yet been committed. The exact-address proof addresses that separate cross-lane dependency before the scan-first path is used.
Should I phrase this as proving the exit lane will always match scalar?

Keep it as a hypothesis: if the dereference-free, exact-address proof correctly excludes every relevant earlier-store/later-predicate overlap, then this particular reason for a precommit scan to change the exit lane is removed; otherwise, fall back to scalar. The statement does not establish that the proof is implementable in every case or that all other correctness conditions have been verified.
Does it also establish that masked loads cannot fault incorrectly?

No. The hypothesis restricts how the precommit exit scan is admitted; it does not replace the separate requirement to keep loads within scalar-reachable operations and preserve precise faults. A proof about store-to-predicate overlap is not, on its own, a proof about every load or fault.
So the fallback is mandatory whenever the proof is unavailable, even if the chunk might in fact be safe?

Under the proposed rule, yes. Safety that has not been established by the required dereference-free exact-address proof does not qualify the chunk for the precommit scan. Scalar fallback covers cases where the proof fails or cannot be obtained, without claiming that every such case contains a harmful overlap.

I want to make the next step concrete: prove cross-lane addresses without dereferencing memory, prove that the exit-predicate loads are safe, scan predicates sequentially, scalarize cases that cannot be proved, and rerun ExitAlias-12.

That is a plan for deciding when the precommit scan may be used, then checking its behavior. The cross-lane address proof concerns whether an earlier store can overlap a later exit-predicate load. Predicate-load safety is a separate condition: establishing addresses does not, by itself, authorize reading those addresses. Cases for which the necessary proofs cannot be made would use scalar execution, and ExitAlias-12 would be rerun to assess the resulting behavior.
Why keep the address proof and predicate-load safety proof separate?

They answer different questions. The address proof asks whether a cross-lane store-to-predicate-load overlap can be excluded without dereferencing memory. Predicate-load safety asks whether performing the predicate loads during the scan respects scalar execution, including its exit boundary and fault behavior. Knowing that two addresses do not overlap does not establish that both loads are permitted to occur.
Does “dereference-free cross-lane addresses” mean the proof may calculate an address but not read the memory at it?

Nonoverlap addresses the possibility that an earlier store changes what a later predicate load observes. Predicate-load safety is needed alongside the cross-lane proof, not inferred from it.

No. Sequential scanning preserves the order in which exit predicates are considered. It cannot make an unproved memory access safe, and it cannot make a later predicate load observe an earlier store that has not taken effect. The proofs determine whether this scan can be used for the case at hand.

It does not. It specifies what must be proved—dereference-free cross-lane addresses and predicate-load safety—and what happens when proof is unavailable. No particular address-analysis method or proof procedure is stated.
