The guarded scan has to be justified under the required ordering.
Does the proposal specify what the predicate guards prove?

It says to scalar-scan guarded predicates, but does not define a particular guard or proof procedure. Whatever guards are used must make the scan consistent with scalar semantics; the proposal alone does not establish that they cover every aliasing or faulting case.
Could the scan itself access memory beyond the scalar exit while trying to discover where the exit is?

It must not. A scan that reads a later predicate after scalar execution would have exited would violate the no-access requirement, regardless of whether the later result is discarded. Discovering the exit cannot rely on performing memory accesses that scalar execution would never perform.
When the prefix is exit-free, does that automatically mean its stores may be issued all at once?

No. The proposal explicitly says to commit stores in order. An exit-free prefix establishes a stopping-point property, not freedom to change the observable order of potentially aliasing writes. Vectorizing eligible work and preserving the scalar-observable store sequence remain separate obligations.
How should I understand an “uncertain tail” without assuming it definitely contains an exit or a fault?

Uncertain means the conditions needed to put that tail on the vectorized path have not been established. It does not assert that the tail actually exits, aliases, or faults. Scalarizing it avoids relying on an unproved claim about what may be accessed or reordered.
Does scalarizing the tail allow it to start anywhere?

It still has to continue from the point reached under scalar semantics. The eligible prefix and the scalar tail must fit together without skipping an iteration that scalar execution would perform or revisiting effects already committed. The proposal does not specify the mechanics of that transition.
Is an exit encountered during the scan part of the vectorized prefix?

An exit-free prefix, by definition, cannot include an exit decision that stops execution within it. Which operations in an exiting iteration scalar execution performs depends on their order in that loop, and the proposal does not specify that order. Those operations cannot simply be assumed eligible for vectorization on the strength of the exit-free-prefix description.
Could I claim this arrangement resolves every potential alias between a store and a predicate load?

No. The guarded predicate scan must still respect any earlier-store/later-predicate-load dependency. Committing the vectorized prefix’s stores in order does not, by itself, justify reading a later predicate before a store it should observe. The proposal identifies a way to partition execution, but the guards and scheduling would still have to meet that condition.
What about precise faults if the prefix is dereferenceable?

Dereferenceability is one necessary condition for the proposed vectorized prefix, but precise faults concern the behavior and ordering of actual memory accesses relative to scalar execution. The predicate scan and scalar tail also have to preserve that behavior. The proposal does not claim fault validation has already been completed.
If a tail could have been safe to vectorize, is scalarizing it contrary to the goal?

Not to the semantic requirement: scalar execution can retain behavior when vector eligibility is uncertain. It may affect the separate performance goal, though. The target remains 1.3× throughput versus optimized scalar code on three representative loops combining exits and aliasing, and this proposal supplies no measurement against it.
So the vector path is not meant to run on every iteration just because the loop vectorizer exists?

Right. Under this proposal it runs on a prefix only when both the exit-free and dereferenceability conditions are established. Uncertain tails remain scalar, while stores from vectorized work are committed in order. That conditional structure is central to the proposal.
Can we state its intended safety boundary without claiming it has been proved?

The intended boundary is: scalar-scan guarded predicates to identify a prefix scalar execution reaches without exiting; vectorize that prefix only when its memory accesses are established dereferenceable; commit its stores in scalar-observable order; and handle the uncertain remainder scalarly. Whether a concrete implementation maintains that boundary, including precise faults and no accesses beyond the scalar exit, remains to be established.
For the exit-free prefix proposal, what proof would permit batching prefix loads without bypassing earlier aliasing stores or reporting a later-lane fault first?

The proof has to cover two independent kinds of scalar order. For each batched load, it must establish that moving the load does not make it observe memory before an earlier store whose effect scalar execution would have seen. It must also establish that performing the loads as a batch cannot expose a later-lane fault ahead of a fault or other required effect from an earlier scalar operation. Knowing that the prefix is exit-free addresses which iterations are reached, but does not by itself settle either ordering question.
Could I justify the batch just by proving every lane in the prefix is before the exit?

No. Every lane might be reached, yet an earlier store could still change a later load’s value. And within a reached prefix, scalar execution still has an order in which operations and possible faults occur. Reachability is necessary for the proposed prefix, but it is not a license to move its loads ahead of dependencies or faults.
What exactly must be established about a store that precedes one of those loads?

If the load would come after that store in scalar execution but before it in the batched execution, the change in order needs justification. One sufficient kind of justification would be proof that their accesses cannot overlap. More generally, the load must be guaranteed to observe the value it would observe after the earlier store, or the execution must preserve the store-before-load relationship. Potential aliasing cannot simply be ignored.
Is ordered commitment of stores enough to supply that relationship?

Not on its own. Committing stores in their proper order relative to one another does not help a load that was already performed before a store it should have observed. The proof for batching must address the load’s position relative to earlier stores, as well as the order in which stores become observable.
Suppose an earlier store and a later load have different addresses. Is that the sort of fact the proof could use?

Yes—if the fact is established for the accesses actually at issue. Proving that the addresses do not overlap removes that particular store-to-load dependency. Merely assuming that different iterations use different addresses would not suffice when accesses may alias.
Would it be necessary to prove that all stores and loads in the prefix are pairwise disjoint?

The question is narrower than blanket pairwise disjointness. It concerns stores that scalar execution places before a load but batching would move after it. Those are the relationships that must be preserved or shown not to affect the load. Other possible interactions cannot be disregarded if they affect scalar semantics, but this question does not establish that every pair must be disjoint.
How does the fault half of the proof differ from the alias half?

The alias half concerns which value a load observes. The fault half concerns which memory access is allowed to fault first, and what scalar execution would have done before that fault. Even a load with no aliasing store might fault; batching cannot let its lane’s fault appear before an earlier fault that scalar execution would encounter first.
If I know the whole prefix is dereferenceable, does that settle the later-lane fault concern?

If dereferenceability is established for every batched access under the conditions in which it runs, that can rule out faults from those accesses and thus address this particular competition among their faults. But calling a prefix dereferenceable is not itself the proof. The guarantee must cover the actual loads being moved, and it does not automatically settle faults from other operations whose scalar order the batch crosses.
So proving that just the last lane’s address is safe would not be enough?

Correct. A safe last-lane address says nothing about an earlier load that could fault, or another later-lane load that could fault first when batched. The necessary fault argument must account for the relevant accesses and their scalar ordering, not just one boundary address.
What if two loads can both fault, but the batched execution ultimately reports one of those faults?

Reporting a fault from one of them is not necessarily precise. If scalar execution would encounter the other fault first, or would perform observable stores before reaching the reported fault, the batch has changed scalar behavior. The question is which fault scalar execution reaches first and what it has already done at that point.
Does a later-lane fault matter if we never use that lane’s loaded value?

Yes. A fault is an effect of the access, not of using its returned value. Discarding the value cannot undo a fault exposed ahead of scalar order. Nor would discarding it justify an access that scalar execution does not reach.
Is there a distinction between suppressing the report of a fault and not making the load?

There is. Not reporting an incorrectly early fault is only part of preserving precise behavior. The vectorizer also must not access memory beyond the scalar exit. For a load within an exit-free prefix, the separate question remains whether moving its access respects preceding scalar operations and fault order. The proof must concern the actual accesses, not only which outcomes are eventually reported.
Could an earlier store matter to faults as well as to the value loaded?

The required ordering is about scalar execution as a whole. If scalar execution performs a store before reaching a faulting load, reporting that load’s fault before the store takes effect could change the observable state at the fault. Thus the batching argument cannot consider only load-to-load fault order and disregard earlier ordered stores.
How should we treat operations within a single iteration?

Use their actual scalar order. A lane identifies an iteration, but it does not specify where its loads, stores, and exit decision occur within that iteration. The proof must not assume an operation is earlier or later merely from its lane number when the within-iteration order matters.
And does the scalar predicate scan itself need to be considered in that order?

Yes. Scanning predicates scalarly does not automatically make their loads safe to move ahead of earlier stores or faults. The proposed batch must fit around the predicate accesses as scalar execution orders them; otherwise an exit-free result from the scan would not, by itself, justify the memory schedule.
Could a proof allow some prefix loads to be batched while leaving others in scalar order?

Conceptually, yes. The question is whether the loads actually chosen for batching have the needed dependency and fault-order justification. It does not require every load in an exit-free prefix to be batched. Leaving an operation in scalar order is different from claiming it is safe to move.
If I cannot resolve whether an earlier store aliases one of the proposed batched loads, what can I conclude?

You cannot conclude that the load may bypass that store. The unresolved alias leaves open a scalar-observable value dependency. The prefix proposal already allows uncertain work to remain scalar; the question does not provide a proof that would make this particular move safe.
Likewise, what if I cannot establish whether an earlier operation might fault?

Then you cannot simply assume a later-lane load may expose its fault first. You would need a way to preserve the scalar-first fault and preceding effects, or refrain from the reordering that creates the risk. No such mechanism or completed proof is specified here.
Would a correct final value for every load be sufficient evidence for batching?

No. Correct loaded values would not establish that faults were precise, that earlier stores had become observable in the right order, or that no forbidden memory access occurred. The batching proof must cover the ordering of effects and accesses, not just the values eventually computed.
Can you give a compact statement of the proof obligation without prescribing an implementation?

For each load moved into the batch, establish that it is scalar-reachable and permitted to access, that moving it does not bypass an earlier store whose effect it must observe, and that its execution cannot make a later scalar-order fault appear before an earlier fault or required write. If any of those conditions remains unresolved, the exit-free prefix alone does not justify batching that load.
Does that answer mean the proposed prefix strategy is already correct or incorrect?

Neither conclusion follows from the question. It identifies what must be proved before batching prefix loads is compatible with the scalar-semantics goal. No proof, implementation result, or throughput measurement is supplied here.

Here is my hypothesis for prefix-load batching: batch only when dereference-free checks prove that the prefix loads cannot fault or overlap preceding writes. Otherwise, execute the lanes in scalar order.

That gives batching a conditional safety boundary. The checks must establish both properties for the loads being batched: they cannot fault, and they cannot overlap writes that precede them in scalar order. If either property cannot be proved without dereferencing memory, the hypothesis calls for scalar-order lane execution rather than batching. It is a proposed rule, not a verified result.
Why do I need both conditions? Would proving that the loads cannot fault be enough?

No. A nonfaulting load could still read a value different from scalar execution if batching moves it ahead of a preceding write to the same location. The nonoverlap condition addresses that store-to-load dependency; the nonfaulting condition addresses the risk of exposing a fault from a batched load out of scalar order.
And if I prove nonoverlap with preceding writes, can I ignore the fault condition?

No. A load can be independent of preceding writes and still fault. Batching it with other loads could then expose its fault before scalar execution would reach it. The proposed permission to batch requires both proofs.
Does “preceding writes” refer to writes before the whole prefix, or writes earlier in scalar execution than a particular load?

The relevant relationship is scalar order relative to each proposed batched load. A write that scalar execution performs before that load cannot be bypassed if the two accesses overlap. The hypothesis does not supply a loop layout, so it would be too narrow to interpret “preceding” solely as writes outside the prefix.
What if a preceding write and a load overlap, but the write happens to leave the loaded value unchanged?

Under this hypothesis, that load does not qualify for batching on the strength of the stated checks: the required proof excludes overlap, not merely a change in value. The fallback to scalar-order lanes avoids depending on a particular overlapping write being harmless.
I want “cannot overlap” to mean something stronger than not seeing an overlap in one run.

Yes. It is a proof obligation for the loads and preceding writes on the path that takes the batch. Merely failing to observe an overlap would not establish that one cannot occur. Where the check cannot prove nonoverlap, the stated response is scalar-order execution.
What does the dereference-free qualifier contribute?

It keeps the checks from performing the very memory accesses whose safety they are supposed to establish. A check cannot first issue a proposed load, find that it did not fault, and then use that observation to justify having issued it. The hypothesis requires the no-fault and nonoverlap conclusions to be established without dereferencing memory as part of those checks.
So computing information about an address is different from reading that address?

Conceptually, yes. A dereference-free check can reason about whether accesses would be safe and overlap without itself performing the proposed memory access. The hypothesis does not specify how that reasoning is implemented or guarantee that it will be possible in every case.
If the check cannot establish whether a prefix load can fault, but the load happens not to fault when eventually executed, may it be batched?

Not under the proposed rule. The decision to batch requires a prior proof that the load cannot fault. An unknown outcome is not such a proof, even if a later scalar execution of the load turns out to succeed.
And an unresolved possible overlap gets the same treatment?

Yes. If nonoverlap with preceding writes cannot be proved, the hypothesis says to execute the lanes in scalar order. That does not claim an overlap exists; it says the permission to batch has not been established.
Why specify scalar order for the lanes rather than simply discard a batched result when a problem appears?

Discarding a result would not undo an already performed memory access or an incorrectly early fault. It would also not repair a value read before a preceding write whose effect scalar execution would have observed. Executing lanes in scalar order avoids relying on those speculative batched accesses when the required proofs are unavailable.
Does scalar-order lane execution mean there can be no fault?

No. A load that scalar execution reaches may fault, and preserving that fault is part of scalar semantics. The distinction is that scalar-order execution does not let a later lane’s batched load report its fault before the earlier scalar operations that should precede it.
If the checks prove every batched load cannot fault, does that prove the entire prefix cannot fault?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis concerns the prefix loads selected for batching. It does not state that every other operation in the prefix is nonfaulting. Any other potentially faulting operation still has to respect scalar semantics; the proposed proof should not be described as covering more than the loads it actually addresses.
Likewise, does proving nonoverlap with preceding writes prove that all memory accesses in the prefix are disjoint?

No. It rules out the specified overlap between batched prefix loads and writes preceding those loads in scalar order. It does not assert pairwise disjointness for every access, or remove the separate requirement to commit stores in observable order.
What if only some prefix loads satisfy both proofs?

The hypothesis permits batching only loads for which the conditions are proved. It does not say that an entire prefix must be batched merely because some loads qualify. Any lanes or work for which the needed conditions remain uncertain must retain scalar-order execution under the stated fallback rule.
Could I describe the checks as a way to discover the first faulting lane?

That would misstate the hypothesis. The checks are meant to prove that loads admitted to a batch cannot fault at all; they do not discover a fault by performing the loads or select which fault to report. If that no-fault proof cannot be made, execution proceeds in scalar lane order.
Does the no-fault proof let batching ignore the scalar exit?

No. It is a condition for batching prefix loads, not permission to access iterations beyond the scalar exit. The loads must still belong to a prefix scalar execution reaches. A load could be nonfaulting yet still be forbidden if scalar execution exits before it.
Would it be accurate to say these checks replace the scalar predicate scan?

No. The proposal distinguishes establishing an exit-free prefix from establishing that its loads can safely be batched. Dereference-free no-fault and nonoverlap checks address the batching question; they do not, by themselves, determine where a data-dependent exit occurs.
How does this hypothesis address the concern about a later-lane fault being reported first?

If every load admitted to the batch is proved unable to fault, none of those batched loads can report a later-lane fault first. Where that proof is unavailable, executing lanes in scalar order avoids introducing a batched load fault ahead of the order in which scalar execution would encounter it. This addresses that specific risk without claiming all other fault-order questions have been resolved.
And the concern about bypassing an earlier aliasing store?

The required nonoverlap proof excludes an earlier scalar-order write from aliasing a load moved into the batch. If that exclusion cannot be proved, scalar-order execution retains the relevant write-before-load order. A load is not admitted to the batch merely because its result can be computed or discarded.
Can I say this achieves the throughput target?

No. The hypothesis states when batching would be permitted and what to do otherwise; it contains no throughput measurements. Proof checks and scalar-order execution can affect performance, so reaching 1.3× throughput versus optimized scalar code on the three representative loops remains a separate question.
Then what is the narrow claim I should make?

The proposed rule is: batch prefix loads only when dereference-free checks prove those loads cannot fault or overlap preceding scalar-order writes; otherwise execute the lanes in scalar order. That is a hypothesis for avoiding the specified alias and early-fault hazards, not a claim that the checks have been implemented, that every semantic condition is proved, or that a speedup has been measured.
I want to benchmark guarded-prefix batching with scalar tails on ExitAlias-12 and the three kernels. The comparisons should cover exits, store traces, first faults, and throughput.

That activity tests both the semantic behavior and the performance of the guarded-prefix approach. For ExitAlias-12 and the three kernels, exits, store traces, and first faults can be compared with scalar execution. Throughput can be compared with the optimized-scalar baseline relevant to the 1.3× target. No outcome of these comparisons is stated yet.
Why include ExitAlias-12 as well as the three kernels?

They serve different parts of the evaluation. ExitAlias-12 provides differential cases for examining exit and memory-order behavior, while the three kernels are the setting for the stated throughput target. Running guarded-prefix batching with scalar tails on both avoids trying to infer performance on the kernels solely from a differential-test count, or semantic behavior solely from a speed measurement.
What precisely should an exit comparison tell us?

It asks whether the guarded-prefix execution stops where scalar execution stops. A prefix selected for batching must not cross the scalar exit, and the scalar tail must continue the execution that remains. Matching eventual output without matching the exit would not resolve that question.
Could an exit match hide a write-order error?

Yes. Two executions can identify the same exit yet perform writes in different observable orders. Comparing store traces separately checks the sequence of stores against scalar execution, rather than assuming an exit match or equal final memory contents establishes ordered commits.
What does comparing first faults add beyond recording whether a fault happened?

The first fault matters because scalar execution has an order in which it reaches operations. A batched load must not expose a later-lane fault ahead of an earlier scalar-order fault or other required effects. Comparing the first fault with scalar execution therefore probes precision more directly than a simple yes-or-no fault count. A run with no fault should not be described as having a matching fault address.
If the first faults match, have we proved that no extra memory access occurred?

No. An access beyond the scalar exit might not fault. Matching first faults is an important observable check, but it does not by itself prove that every memory access stayed within the scalar-reachable portion of the loop.
How do scalar tails affect the interpretation of a result?

They are part of the guarded-prefix approach being evaluated, not work to exclude from the comparison. A semantic match could involve a batched prefix followed by scalar execution, and the measured throughput would reflect that combination. The activity does not say how often batching or scalar tails occur.
Would a matching result on a case that ran entirely scalarly demonstrate that batching is safe?

No. It would establish the reported match for that execution, but would not exercise batched prefix loads in that case. To interpret an observed match as evidence about batching, one must distinguish the behavior of executions that actually take a batched path from those handled scalarly; this activity does not yet supply that distinction or any results.
Does “guarded-prefix batching” imply we can load all lanes in a chunk and discard the ones after the exit?

No. The intended batching is confined to a prefix established as reachable and eligible. Discarding values from later lanes would not undo their memory accesses or faults. Scalar tails remain the proposed treatment for work whose eligibility has not been established.
What is the connection between this benchmark and the proposed no-fault and nonoverlap checks?

The benchmark evaluates an approach in which batching is conditional on dereference-free checks proving that admitted prefix loads cannot fault or overlap preceding writes; otherwise lanes execute in scalar order. Exit, store-trace, and first-fault comparisons test consequences of getting that boundary wrong. A match in the tested executions would be evidence about them, not a universal proof that every check is sufficient.
Would an early fault in a batched prefix necessarily show up in the first-fault comparison?

If it changes which fault is first relative to scalar execution, that comparison is designed to expose the difference. But the reported activity has no results yet, and fault comparisons alone do not detect every possible forbidden access, especially one that does not fault.
If throughput looks good but a store trace differs, how should I treat the speed number?

Report the measurement as a measurement, but not as satisfying the vectorizer’s goal. The goal requires scalar-observable write ordering as well as performance. A faster execution with a different store trace would leave the correctness requirement unmet.
Conversely, would matching exits, stores, and first faults establish the 1.3× target?

No. Those are semantic comparisons. Throughput is a separate observation and must be measured against optimized scalar code on the three representative loops. ExitAlias-12 agreement cannot be converted into a speedup figure for the kernels.
Does the activity specify whether each kernel must reach 1.3× or whether the three are aggregated?

It calls for comparing throughput on three kernels, while the goal states a 1.3× target against optimized scalar code on three representative loops. No aggregation rule is supplied here. The activity should not be described as having passed or failed a particular per-kernel or combined interpretation before measurements and a reporting rule are available.
Should I assume the scalar tails are small because only uncertain work reaches them?

No. “Uncertain” explains why that work is kept scalar; it does not quantify its size or frequency. The benchmark is needed precisely because the relative cost of batched prefixes, guards, and scalar tails cannot be read from the proposal alone.
Could identical throughput between two runs tell us anything about whether the first fault is precise?
Not by itself. Throughput measures performance, whereas the first-fault comparison addresses scalar fault order. The measurements are complementary, and neither should stand in for the other.
How should I phrase this activity without anticipating a favorable result?

Benchmark guarded-prefix batching with scalar tails on ExitAlias-12 and the three kernels; compare exits, store traces, and first faults against scalar execution, and record throughput against optimized scalar code. That states what will be evaluated without claiming that the semantics match or that throughput reaches 1.3×.

The guarded-prefix results are in. ExitAlias-12 matched scalar exit lanes, store traces, and first faults, with zero accesses beyond the scalar exit. The three guarded-prefix speedups were 1.34×, 1.38×, and 1.32×.

Those results report both semantic observations and performance. On ExitAlias-12, the recorded exit lanes, store traces, and first faults matched scalar execution, and the access check found zero beyond-exit accesses. For the three kernels, the guarded-prefix speedups were 1.34×, 1.38×, and 1.32× relative to optimized scalar code. The figures are reported separately; no combined speedup is given.
What does matching exit lanes establish in the ExitAlias-12 result?

It establishes that the guarded-prefix executions selected the same stopping lanes as scalar execution in those tests. That matters because the exit determines which subsequent loop operations scalar execution reaches. An exit-lane match is an important observation, but it does not stand in for the separate store, fault, and memory-access results.
Why report the store traces separately if the exits matched?

The same stopping lane does not guarantee the same observable sequence of writes. The matching store traces report that the recorded writes followed the scalar trace in ExitAlias-12, rather than merely leaving the same final memory contents.
Does a matching first fault mean every test case faulted?

No. It means first-fault behavior matched scalar execution in the ExitAlias-12 comparison. A case in which neither execution faults can agree on that observation too. The result does not provide a case-by-case list of faults.
And it would be too much to claim that every possible later fault matched, correct?
Correct. The stated comparison is of first faults. It should not be expanded into an unreported comparison of every possible fault after the first one.
I’m particularly interested in the zero beyond-exit accesses. How is that different from seeing no unexpected guard-page fault?

It is a stronger reported observation about the ExitAlias-12 executions: zero accesses were recorded beyond the scalar exit. An access beyond the exit could be forbidden even if it did not fault, so merely observing no unexpected fault would not convey the same result.
Can I extend that zero-access claim to every loop the vectorizer might process?
No. The zero beyond-exit accesses are reported for ExitAlias-12. They are evidence about those tested executions, not a universal statement about all loops or inputs.
Do the numbers tell us which of the three kernels had which speedup?

They give three speedups—1.34×, 1.38×, and 1.32×—but do not name the individual kernels or describe their workloads. You can report the three figures without assigning additional characteristics to any one of them.
Should those figures be described as throughput relative to optimized scalar code, rather than as reductions in execution time?

Yes. The stated comparison uses optimized scalar code as its baseline, and the figures are speedup ratios for the guarded-prefix approach. Describing them as 34%, 38%, and 32% higher throughput than that baseline is consistent with the ratios; describing them as those same percentages less execution time would not be equivalent.
Does the ExitAlias-12 agreement show how often a prefix was batched rather than handled by the scalar tail?

No. The result reports the observable comparisons and zero beyond-exit accesses, but no batching frequency or scalar-tail count. Neither should be inferred from the semantic matches or from the three speedup figures.
Is it fair to say these observations bear on the proposed no-fault and nonoverlap conditions without calling them a proof for all executions?

Yes. Matching first faults and store traces, together with matching exits and zero beyond-exit accesses in ExitAlias-12, are evidence that the guarded-prefix executions in those tests maintained the reported scalar observations. They do not, by themselves, prove that every dereference-free check is sufficient for every possible execution.
Could I say the three speedups also establish that the three kernels had matching scalar store traces and first faults?

Not from this result as written. The scalar exit-lane, store-trace, first-fault, and beyond-exit-access findings are reported for ExitAlias-12; the three numerical speedups are reported for the guarded-prefix kernels. The speedup figures alone do not supply separate semantic comparisons for each kernel.
Then what is the cleanest way to report the outcome without merging the two sets of observations?

Report them side by side: ExitAlias-12 matched scalar exit lanes, store traces, and first faults and recorded zero accesses beyond the scalar exit; guarded-prefix throughput on the three kernels was 1.34×, 1.38×, and 1.32× optimized scalar. That preserves the scope of each reported observation.
How can guards prove prefix loads nonfaulting when pointer provenance is unknown, without speculative dereferences or assumptions about page mappings?

Unknown provenance alone does not supply that proof. A guard would need some independently justified fact about each load’s access—one established without performing the load or assuming that its address is mapped. If no such fact is available, the guard cannot soundly classify the load as nonfaulting for batching. That does not mean the load will fault; it means its safety has not been proved.
Is checking the numerical address enough to establish that fact?

Not by itself. An address calculation can identify where a load would attempt to read without establishing that the access is valid and nonfaulting. In particular, knowing an address’s value is different from knowing what memory access that pointer is permitted to make.
What if the calculated addresses for all prefix lanes fall in a tidy range?

A range of calculated addresses still needs a justified safety guarantee covering the actual loads. The shape of the range does not establish pointer provenance or nonfaulting access on its own. The guard also cannot obtain that guarantee by reading the range first and treating the absence of a fault as proof that the reads were permissible.
That last point is the speculative-dereference concern, right?

Yes. If a guard performs a proposed load to discover whether it faults, the potentially incorrect access has already happened. Suppressing its value or choosing scalar execution afterward would not undo an early fault or an access scalar execution would not have reached. A dereference-free proof must precede the load it authorizes.
Could a guard rely on the fact that a page appears to be mapped?

Not under the constraint in your question. A page-mapping assumption is not the requested provenance and nonfaulting proof. It also should not be silently substituted for a guarantee about the actual load. The question calls for justification that does not depend on assuming anything about page mappings.
So what sort of information could make the proof possible in principle?

In principle, an independently established guarantee that the particular accesses are valid and nonfaulting could support it—for example, a guarantee about the memory region and the accesses within it, if one actually applies. That is a statement about what a proof would need, not a claim that the vectorizer has such a guarantee for these pointers or that a particular way of obtaining one has been chosen.
If pointer provenance is unknown, wouldn't asserting a region guarantee simply assume away the problem?

It would if the guarantee were merely asserted. The guard must derive it from information legitimately available for the execution. If that information is absent, renaming an address range as a safe region does not establish nonfaulting loads.
Does being in an exit-free prefix help with provenance?

It helps with a different obligation: establishing that scalar execution reaches the prefix before exiting. It does not establish that a pointer used by a reached load is safe to dereference. Scalar execution can reach a load and fault there, so reachability and nonfaulting access must not be conflated.
Could the scalar predicate scan provide the missing proof?

Only if the scan establishes a relevant memory-safety fact without making an impermissible access; being a scalar scan does not inherently establish one. It can help identify the exit-free portion, but it does not automatically prove that all other loads in that portion cannot fault.
What if the scalar loop itself would eventually perform every load in that prefix?

That establishes reachability if the prefix and operation ordering have been identified correctly, but it does not establish that those loads will all complete without fault. Scalar execution might encounter a fault at one of them. Batching cannot expose a later load’s fault ahead of the first fault scalar execution would encounter.
Is that why the proposed batching condition asks for nonfaulting loads rather than merely scalar-reachable loads?

Yes. If every load admitted to a batch is genuinely proved nonfaulting, those loads cannot compete to produce an incorrectly early later-lane fault. The proof still has to apply to the loads actually batched; the label “prefix” cannot substitute for it.
Suppose a guard can prove the addresses of two loads are different. Does that contribute to the nonfaulting proof?

Different addresses may help with an overlap question, but they do not show that either address is safe to read. The guard’s nonoverlap and nonfaulting obligations are distinct. Resolving one cannot be treated as resolving the other.
Likewise, could proving that a load does not overlap a preceding write make it safe to batch even if it might fault?

No. That proof would address whether moving the load bypasses the write’s effect. It would leave the fault-order risk unresolved. Under the proposed batching condition, a load needs both a nonoverlap proof for relevant preceding writes and a nonfaulting proof.
Would it help to perform the unknown-provenance loads one lane at a time to find out whether they fault?

Executing them in scalar order is different from proving them nonfaulting ahead of a batch. A load performed when scalar execution reaches it can fault at the appropriate point. Its successful execution does not retroactively authorize speculative loads from later lanes, and a fault stops the execution according to scalar order.
Does that mean unknown provenance necessarily forces the entire loop to remain scalar?

Not necessarily. The limitation applies to loads for which the required nonfaulting proof is unavailable. It does not establish that every load in the loop lacks a proof or that no other work could be handled differently. The question does not provide enough information to decide how much, if any, work qualifies for batching.
Could a guard check only the first and last prefix addresses and infer that everything between them is safe?

Not without a justified guarantee covering the intervening accesses. Safety at two addresses does not, on its own, prove that every proposed load between them is valid and nonfaulting—particularly when the pointers’ provenance is unknown. Nor could the guard establish safety at the endpoints through speculative reads.
Should the proof be understood as covering a pointer in the abstract or each memory access it is used for?

It must cover the accesses proposed for batching. A general statement that a pointer has a numerical value is not enough; the nonfaulting conclusion has to apply to each actual load under the conditions in which the batch executes. The question gives no particular pointer guarantee from which to derive that conclusion.
What if a check returns “unknown” rather than “unsafe”?

“Unknown” is not proof that the load would fault, but it is also not proof that it cannot fault. It cannot satisfy the condition for admitting that load to a batch. Executing the uncertain lanes in scalar order preserves the distinction between an unproved access and an access known to be invalid.
Can a later successful scalar load be used to argue that batching it earlier would have been harmless?

Not generally. Success when scalar execution reaches the load does not establish that performing it earlier preserves the order of preceding writes and faults, or that an earlier speculative access would have been permitted before the exit was known. The proof for batching has to justify the changed execution order in advance.
What is the narrow answer to the original question, then?

A dereference-free guard can prove unknown-provenance prefix loads nonfaulting only if it has an independently justified safety guarantee that covers those particular loads; numerical addresses and page-mapping assumptions do not supply one. If the guarantee cannot be established, nonfaulting batching is unproved, and the uncertain loads must retain scalar-order execution under the proposed rule. No such guarantee or completed guard proof is specified here.

Here’s the plan for the provenance problem: batch loads only within proven dereferenceable object bounds, using checked offsets. Scalarize pointers whose provenance is unknown, and verify fault ordering with guard pages.

That gives the batching decision a concrete boundary. A load qualifies only when the applicable object bounds are proved dereferenceable and its offset is checked to stay within them. Unknown-provenance pointers take the scalar path rather than being treated as safe because their numerical addresses look plausible. Guard-page tests then check fault ordering against scalar execution. This is a plan, not a report that the checks or tests have succeeded.
What must the checked offset establish?

It must establish that the proposed load stays within the proven dereferenceable bounds for the object. The check must cover the memory access actually being batched, not just the location of an address calculated for it. The plan does not specify a particular arithmetic procedure for making that check.
Is knowing an object's bounds enough without checking the offset?

No. Proven bounds identify the region that may be dereferenced; the checked offset connects a particular load to that region. Without that connection, the existence of a dereferenceable object would not show that the load accesses it within its bounds.
And checking an offset against a range that has not been proved dereferenceable would not be enough either?

Right. An in-range calculation is not, by itself, a proof that the underlying memory access is valid. The plan requires both a proven dereferenceable object bound and a checked offset for the load admitted to the batch.
I don't want the offset check to become a speculative read.

It should not. The check is meant to justify a later batched memory access, not perform that access to see whether it succeeds. If checking the offset required dereferencing the uncertain pointer, it would not resolve the concern about speculative dereferences.
How should unknown pointer provenance affect path selection?

Under this plan, an unknown-provenance pointer is scalarized. That is a response to the lack of a qualifying proof, not a finding that the pointer necessarily points outside an object or will fault when scalar execution reaches it.
Could an unknown-provenance pointer happen to refer to mapped memory and still be scalarized?
Yes. Whether its address happens to be mapped is not the proof this plan requires. Scalarizing it avoids relying on a page-mapping assumption or on the absence of a fault from a speculative load.
Does scalarizing that pointer mean we omit its load?

No. It means performing the relevant work in scalar order when scalar execution reaches it. If scalar execution would perform the load, it remains part of the execution and may fault there; if scalar execution exits before it, the load must not be performed.
Does a checked offset make a load safe even if the scalar loop exits before reaching it?

No. The bounds-and-offset proof addresses dereferenceability, not reachability. Batching is still limited by the scalar exit: a load cannot be performed merely because its address is within a dereferenceable object if scalar execution would stop first.
What if several loads are in the same proven object? Can I treat all of them as one checked access?

The proof must cover every access actually included in the batch. Sharing a proven object does not dispense with checking that each load's offset puts its entire access within the applicable dereferenceable bounds. The plan does not specify a combined check that would make those individual obligations disappear.
I also want to avoid claiming that these bounds checks settle aliasing with earlier stores.

That distinction is important. Staying inside a dereferenceable object can support a nonfaulting argument for a load, but it does not show that the load cannot overlap an earlier write in that object. Any batching that moves a load ahead of a preceding scalar-order write still needs its separate ordering justification.
So this plan addresses the unknown-provenance fault concern, but does not replace the other batching condition?

Exactly. Proven dereferenceable object bounds and checked offsets supply the proposed route to establishing that eligible loads can be batched without faulting. They do not, on their own, establish the absence of preceding-write overlap, an exit-free prefix, or ordered store commitment.
What is guard-page verification supposed to tell us?

It is intended to expose fault-order mistakes in tested executions. Comparing the first fault and its location with scalar execution can show whether batching reports a fault that scalar execution would encounter later—or would not encounter at all. Guard pages are a validation tool, not a substitute for proving the bounds and checking the offsets before batching.
If a guard-page test produces no fault, does that prove the pointer has known provenance?

No. A successful access in a test does not establish provenance or a general nonfaulting guarantee. Under the plan, unknown-provenance pointers remain scalarized even if a particular tested access does not fault.
Could matching fault order on the guard-page tests prove that every possible fault is ordered correctly?

No. A match would be evidence for the executions tested. It would not cover every possible pointer, offset, exit decision, or access order. The plan calls for verification with guard pages; it does not claim a universal result from them.
Why look at ordering rather than simply count how many faults occur?

Precise scalar behavior depends on which fault occurs first and what execution has reached by then. Two versions could both fault yet differ because one accesses a later lane prematurely. Comparing fault order against scalar execution is therefore more informative than a fault count alone.
Should the bounds proof be made before issuing the batched loads?

Yes. The checked offsets and proven dereferenceable bounds are prerequisites for batching under this plan. Performing the loads first and checking afterward would not prevent an early fault or undo an access beyond the scalar exit.
If an offset check cannot establish that a load remains in the proven bounds, should I describe it as a fault?

No. A failed or unavailable proof is not necessarily a fault in scalar execution. The plan calls for scalarizing that uncertain work, allowing the scalar-order access—if reached—to determine its actual behavior.
Does the plan say how often these proofs will be available, or whether batching still reaches 1.3× throughput?

It does not. It specifies when batching is permitted, what to do with unknown-provenance pointers, and how to verify fault ordering with guard pages. It gives no proof-availability counts or throughput measurements against optimized scalar code.
Can you state the narrow intended rule without treating validation as complete?

Batch a load only if proven dereferenceable object bounds and checked offsets cover its access; execute unknown-provenance pointers scalarly, and use guard-page tests to compare fault ordering with scalar execution. Those are planned conditions and checks, not completed results or permission to relax exit, aliasing, or write-order requirements.

The next activity is to implement checked-offset provenance guards and run the guard-page ProvenanceFault-24 test across bounded and unknown pointers. I want to compare fault order and access traces with scalar execution.

That tests whether the guards admit memory accesses only when their checked offsets support the required provenance and bounds argument. Running ProvenanceFault-24 with guard pages across both bounded and unknown pointers lets you compare not just which fault appears, but the sequence of accesses leading up to it, against scalar execution. This describes the implementation and test activity; it does not report an outcome.
Why compare access traces as well as fault order?

A memory access can be impermissible even if it does not fault. An access trace can reveal an extra or reordered access that a fault comparison alone would miss. Fault order addresses whether a fault is reported at the point scalar execution would encounter it; the trace addresses what memory the execution actually accessed and when.
Could the traces reveal a load beyond the scalar exit even when no guard page is touched?

Yes, if the recorded traces include that access. The no-access-beyond-exit condition applies whether or not the address faults. Comparing the access sequence with scalar execution is therefore useful alongside guard pages, which can make some incorrect accesses observable as faults.
What should “bounded pointers” mean for this test? Does the label alone authorize batching?

No. The relevant question is whether a proposed access is covered by proven dereferenceable object bounds and a checked offset. Calling a pointer bounded does not, by itself, prove that every offset or every proposed load is within those bounds. The guards being implemented must make that connection for accesses they admit.
And how should unknown pointers be treated in the comparison?

The plan is to keep unknown-provenance pointers in scalar order rather than batch their loads on an unproved safety assumption. The test can compare their resulting fault order and access traces with scalar execution. Unknown provenance does not mean an access necessarily faults; it means the guard lacks the specified proof for batching it.
Suppose an unknown pointer points to accessible memory during a test. Would that establish that batching it was safe?

No. A successful access in one execution does not establish a dereferenceable-object guarantee for a speculative batch, nor does it justify moving the access ahead of scalar-order operations. The activity compares behavior across tested pointers; it does not turn an unknown-provenance pointer into a proven one merely because it happens not to fault.
What is a checked-offset guard meant to decide before any batched access occurs?

It is meant to establish that the access proposed for batching falls within the applicable proven dereferenceable object bounds. That decision has to precede the batched load. Reading the memory first and checking afterward would not prevent an early fault or an access that scalar execution would never make.
Does this activity specify how the guards obtain the object bounds?

No. It calls for implementing checked-offset provenance guards but does not specify a source of bounds information or an implementation technique. The test can evaluate the resulting behavior without assuming a particular way the guards establish their premises.
Why use guard pages if access traces are being recorded?

They provide complementary observations. Guard pages can make an incorrectly ordered or unintended access produce a fault, while traces can reveal accesses even when they do not fault. Comparing both with scalar execution gives a clearer view of whether the guarded execution respects the scalar access sequence and fault order.
If both versions fault, what must be compared?

The order matters: the guarded execution must not report a fault from a later scalar-order access before one scalar execution encounters earlier. The access traces can also show what each execution did before that fault. Simply recording that both faulted would not establish agreement.
What if scalar execution doesn't fault for a particular tested pointer?

Then a fault in the guarded execution would be a discrepancy. If neither faults, their access traces still matter: matching absence of a fault does not establish that the guarded execution avoided extra accesses or preserved access order.
Can I interpret a matching fault order as proof that the checked-offset guards prevent all speculative dereferences?

Not by itself. A speculative access might not fault, and fault order says nothing about an unobserved access unless the access trace captures it. Even matching fault order and traces in ProvenanceFault-24 would be evidence for the tested executions, not a proof about every possible pointer and offset.
Does an access trace also help distinguish a guard's check from a speculative load?

It can help identify whether a memory access occurred while deciding to take a guarded path, provided the trace records that access. The check is supposed to establish safety before the load it authorizes; it cannot use an unproved dereference as its own proof. The activity does not specify the trace format or which accesses it records, so its conclusions should track what is actually observed.
Should the scalar comparison include what happens before the first fault, rather than only the faulting address?

Yes. Access traces provide that context. Even if the same faulting access is ultimately reached, performing a later access or skipping an earlier one beforehand could differ from scalar execution. Comparing the sequence leading to the first fault makes the fault-order check more informative.
Does checking provenance and offsets also establish that a load won't overlap a preceding write?

No. Object bounds and checked offsets concern whether the load is justified as nonfaulting. A load within those bounds could still address the same location as a preceding write. Any decision to batch it ahead of that write still needs the separate nonoverlap or ordering justification; ProvenanceFault-24 is described here as comparing fault order and access traces.
If a bounded pointer's offset cannot be verified, is that the same as knowing the access would fault?

No. An unavailable proof does not establish a fault. It means the load cannot qualify for batching under the stated bounds-and-offset condition. Executing it in scalar order, if scalar execution reaches it, allows its actual behavior to occur at the scalar point.
Should we claim ProvenanceFault-24 has found any mismatches yet?

No. The current activity is to implement the checked-offset provenance guards, run ProvenanceFault-24 with guard pages across bounded and unknown pointers, and compare fault order and access traces with scalar execution. It states neither matches nor mismatches.
Does this run provide a new throughput number for the three kernels?

Not as stated. ProvenanceFault-24 is an activity for checking fault order and access traces with the new guards across the specified pointer categories. No throughput benchmark or speedup result is included.
How should I describe the intended outcome without predicting the results?

Describe what will be checked: whether the implemented checked-offset provenance guards keep bounded-pointer accesses within their proven bounds, leave unknown-provenance accesses in scalar order when proof is unavailable, and produce fault order and access traces consistent with scalar execution in the guard-page ProvenanceFault-24 run. Those are evaluation questions, not findings.
ProvenanceFault-24 found 3/24 mismatched first faults. In those cases, predicate scans faulted before earlier stores, even though the batched data loads were nonfaulting.

That identifies a fault-order problem outside the batched data loads themselves. In three of the 24 ProvenanceFault-24 cases, the predicate scan faulted before stores that precede it in scalar execution. The fact that the batched data loads did not fault did not preserve the scalar order of the scan and those stores.
So making the data loads nonfaulting did not settle precise faults for the whole execution?

Correct. It addresses whether those batched data loads can fault, but the predicate scan can also fault. If a scan faults before an earlier scalar-order store has occurred, the execution reaches that fault in a different observable state. The reported 3/24 first-fault mismatches show that this distinction mattered in ProvenanceFault-24.
Is there a contradiction in calling it a scalar predicate scan if it faulted too early?

No. Scanning predicates one at a time can preserve their order relative to one another while still moving them ahead of stores that scalar execution performs first. “Scalar scan” does not, by itself, mean the scan is interleaved with every store in full scalar execution order.
What exactly does “before earlier stores” mean here?

Those stores are earlier than the faulting predicate access in scalar execution. The reported execution let the predicate scan fault before they occurred. It is that reversal—not merely the fact that a predicate load faulted—that creates the discrepancy.
Would committing those stores in order afterward repair the mismatch?

No. Once the predicate scan has faulted, a later ordered commit cannot make the stores have occurred before that fault. Ordering stores relative to one another is not enough if a faulting predicate access has moved ahead of stores that scalar execution places before it.
Does the result mean one of the batched data loads caused each mismatch?

No. The finding specifically attributes the early faults to predicate scans and says the batched data loads were nonfaulting. It would be inaccurate to report these as faults from the batched data loads.
Can I say the checked-offset provenance guards failed to prove the data loads safe?

That is not what this evidence establishes. The reported mismatch concerns predicate scans faulting ahead of earlier stores despite nonfaulting batched data loads. It does not state that a checked offset was wrong or that a batched data load faulted.
Were the three mismatches on bounded pointers or unknown-provenance pointers?
The result does not say. ProvenanceFault-24 covered bounded and unknown pointers, but this finding does not assign the three mismatches to either category.
What can I infer about the other 21 cases?

The reported first-fault mismatch count is 3/24. That does not establish that every other observation—such as access traces, store traces, or exits—matched scalar execution in the remaining cases. Those outcomes are not given here.
Do we know whether the faulting addresses differed from scalar execution?

Not from this report. It identifies mismatched first faults and the fact that predicate scans faulted before earlier stores. It does not give the faulting addresses or a case-by-case account of what the scalar execution faulted on.
If a predicate scan faults at an address scalar execution would eventually read, could it still be wrong?

Yes. Reaching the same address eventually would not make an early fault precise if scalar execution performs observable stores before reaching that predicate access. The reported issue is the fault occurring before those earlier stores, regardless of whether the address might later have been reached.
Does this tell us the predicate scan accessed memory beyond the scalar exit?

No such finding is stated. The reported discrepancy is first-fault ordering relative to earlier stores. It should not be converted into a claim about beyond-exit accesses without an access-trace result showing that.
What about exit lanes? Did these three cases choose wrong exits?
The evidence does not report exit-lane outcomes. A first-fault mismatch is already significant for scalar semantics, but it does not establish a separate exit-lane mismatch.
Is it accurate to say fault ordering must account for predicate loads as well as batched data loads?

Yes. ProvenanceFault-24 shows why restricting attention to faults from batched data loads is insufficient: predicate scans faulted ahead of earlier scalar-order stores in 3/24 cases. Any assessment of precise faults has to account for the predicate accesses and their placement relative to stores too.
Could this result be explained away by saying that stores only matter after a successful scan?

No. In the reported cases, scalar execution orders those stores before the predicate access. Their occurrence before a fault is part of the behavior to preserve. A fault during a scan that was moved ahead of them cannot make those preceding scalar-order stores optional.
Do we have a throughput result from ProvenanceFault-24?
No. The stated result is 3/24 mismatched first faults, with predicate scans faulting before earlier stores despite nonfaulting batched data loads. It supplies no speedup measurement.
What is the most precise way to state what this test exposed?

ProvenanceFault-24 exposed first-fault mismatches in 3/24 cases: predicate scans faulted before stores that scalar execution orders earlier, even though the batched data loads did not fault. That confines the finding to the reported fault-order discrepancy without assuming additional results for exits, access traces, pointer categories, or throughput.
I’m making a conditional decision: retain the 1.32–1.38× guarded-prefix path only when the predicate scans are nonfaulting and independent of preceding stores. Otherwise, scalarize.

That keeps the guarded-prefix path conditional on the predicate scan itself, not just on the batched data loads. Before taking that path, the scan must be established as nonfaulting and independent of stores that precede it in scalar order. If either condition is not established, the decision is to execute scalarly. The 1.32–1.38× range identifies the guarded-prefix performance being retained; it is not a guarantee that every execution under this condition will achieve that speedup.
Why require the predicate scans to be nonfaulting if the batched data loads already satisfy their own no-fault condition?

Because the predicate loads are memory accesses too. A proof that the batched data loads cannot fault says nothing about whether a scan can fault before a store that scalar execution performs earlier. Requiring the scan itself to be nonfaulting addresses that separate source of an incorrectly early fault.
And what does independence from preceding stores protect?

It protects the values used to decide the exit. If a preceding scalar-order store can affect a predicate load, scanning that predicate before the store takes effect could choose a different exit lane. The condition requires that the scan not depend on such a store when the guarded-prefix path is taken.
Would a nonfaulting predicate scan necessarily be independent of those stores?

No. A scan can read successfully yet still see a different value because it was moved ahead of an overlapping store. Nonfaulting access and store independence are separate requirements, and the decision calls for both.
Likewise, if a predicate load is independent of preceding stores, may it still fault?
Yes. Independence says the earlier stores do not affect what it reads; it does not establish that reading is safe. The guarded-prefix path requires a nonfaulting scan as well.
When you say “preceding,” should that be judged by scalar execution order rather than just lane numbers?

Yes. The relevant stores are those scalar execution performs before the predicate access in question. Lane numbers alone do not specify every operation’s order within an iteration. The independence condition must preserve the ordering that matters to scalar behavior.
Does “otherwise scalarize” mean only when we know a predicate will fault or alias a store?

No. If either required condition cannot be established, the guarded-prefix path does not qualify under this decision. Scalarizing an uncertain case does not assert that its predicate actually faults or depends on a preceding store.
Could we take the guarded path first, then switch to scalar if the predicate scan faults?

That would not satisfy this decision. A fault from a scan performed too early has already occurred; switching afterward cannot restore stores that scalar execution would have performed before that fault. The nonfaulting condition must justify taking the path before the scan is moved.
Does scalarizing mean we suppress a faulting predicate load?

No. Scalarization preserves the scalar sequence. If scalar execution reaches the predicate load and it faults, that fault remains part of the behavior, at its scalar-order point. If scalar execution stops before reaching it, the load must not occur.
Could ordered store commits alone satisfy the new condition?

No. Ordering stores relative to one another does not make an earlier scan observe a store that has not happened, and it does not undo a scan fault reported before an earlier scalar-order store. The predicate scan needs its own nonfaulting and independence conditions.
What should I avoid implying with the 1.32–1.38× figure?

Avoid treating it as a promised speedup for every qualifying prefix or for executions that now scalarize. It is the stated performance range associated with the guarded-prefix path, relative to optimized scalar code. This decision limits when that path may be used; it does not supply new measurements after applying the condition.
Does the decision say how we establish that a predicate scan is nonfaulting and independent?
No. It states the conditions for retaining the guarded-prefix path and the scalar alternative. It does not specify a particular proof, guard implementation, or new validation result.
If both predicate conditions hold, are all the other scalar-semantics obligations automatically settled?

No. The conditions address faults and store dependencies of the predicate scan. The execution still has to preserve observable write ordering and precise faults elsewhere, and it must not access memory beyond the scalar exit. Qualifying the scan does not waive those requirements.
So the narrow policy is to admit the fast path only on proof of both scan properties?

Yes. Retain the guarded-prefix path associated with the 1.32–1.38× range only where predicate scans are nonfaulting and independent of preceding scalar-order stores; scalarize otherwise. That is the conditional decision, without claiming new speedups or broader correctness results for the restricted path.

My hypothesis is to batch only exit-free prefixes, and only after proving that both the predicate scans and the loads are nonfaulting and independent of earlier stores. If those conditions cannot be proved, scalarize.

That makes eligibility for batching conditional on the whole proposed scan-and-load sequence, not just the data loads. The prefix must be exit-free, and the predicate scans and loads involved must each be shown not to fault or depend on stores that precede them in scalar order. If a required proof is unavailable, the hypothesis calls for scalar execution rather than batching. It remains a hypothesis, not a demonstrated guarantee.
Why explicitly include the predicate scans in the proof?

Because they perform accesses and make exit decisions. A predicate scan could fault before an earlier scalar-order store, even if every batched data load is nonfaulting. Does “exit-free prefix” mean we can scan any number of predicates ahead and then decide which portion to batch?

No. The scan itself must respect scalar semantics. Calling the resulting portion exit-free does not retroactively justify accesses used to discover it.
What does independence of earlier stores mean for a predicate scan?

It means moving the predicate access into the scan must not change the value used for its exit decision by placing it before a store that scalar execution performs first. And for a load that is batched after the scan?

The same kind of dependency matters. A batched load must not bypass an earlier scalar-order store whose effect it would otherwise observe. Even if the prefix is known to be reached and the load cannot fault, reading it before an affecting store could change the loaded value.
Do I have to prove that every store and load anywhere in the loop is disjoint?

That is broader than the hypothesis states. The proof concerns the predicate scans and loads proposed for the batched path and their dependence on earlier stores. Is proving different addresses one possible way to establish independence?

If it genuinely establishes that the relevant accesses cannot overlap, it can address that particular store-to-load dependency. The hypothesis does not prescribe an address-proof method, and an unresolved possibility of overlap is not a proof of independence.
Suppose an earlier store overlaps a predicate load but happens to leave its value unchanged. Could that predicate still qualify under this hypothesis?

The stated condition is proof of independence from earlier stores, not a guess that a particular overlap will be harmless. Unless the proposed execution can establish that its exit decision remains consistent with scalar order under the dependency, it has not met the condition for batching. Does nonfaulting mean just that no fault was observed in a test?

No. The hypothesis requires a proof that the predicate scans and loads admitted to the path cannot fault under the conditions in which they are performed. An execution that happens not to fault does not establish that guarantee for other executions, or justify having moved a potentially faulting access ahead of scalar-order work.
Why do the loads need a nonfaulting proof if they are all in an exit-free prefix?

An exit-free prefix establishes that scalar execution reaches that portion before an exit. Reaching a load does not mean the load succeeds: scalar execution could fault there. If several loads are batched, a later scalar-order load must not expose its fault before an earlier operation that scalar execution would encounter first. The nonfaulting condition addresses that risk for admitted loads.
Could a nonfaulting predicate scan still be unsafe for the exit decision?

Yes. It may read successfully but read before an earlier store whose value scalar execution would make visible to it. That is why nonfaulting access and independence from earlier stores are separate conditions for predicate scans.
Likewise, could a load be independent of earlier stores but still be ineligible for batching?

Yes. It might lack a nonfaulting proof, or it might not belong to an established exit-free prefix. Independence alone establishes neither that the access can safely be moved into a batch nor that scalar execution reaches it before exiting.
Does the hypothesis require a proof about every operation in a prefix, including stores?

Its stated nonfaulting and independence conditions concern the predicate scans and loads admitted to batching. That does not waive the separate obligation to preserve the observable order of stores, or the precise behavior of any other operation. The hypothesis should not be described as a proof of the entire loop merely because those particular conditions hold.
What if only an initial part of the work satisfies all those conditions?

The hypothesis permits batching only an exit-free prefix for which the required properties have been proved. Work whose eligibility remains uncertain is not admitted merely because some preceding work qualifies; it is scalarized under the stated alternative. The hypothesis does not specify how large a qualifying prefix will be.
If a proof returns “unknown,” is that different from proving that an access will fault or alias?

Yes. Unknown means permission to batch has not been established. It does not mean the access will fault, overlap an earlier store, or cause an exit. Scalarizing in that case preserves scalar order without treating uncertainty as a finding of unsafe behavior.
Could we batch first and switch to scalar if a scan or load faults?

That would not satisfy the proposed condition. An early fault has already occurred, and switching afterward cannot restore preceding stores or undo an access beyond the scalar exit. The relevant nonfaulting and independence proofs must justify the batching before those moved accesses take place.
Does executing scalarly mean a fault is prevented?

No. If scalar execution reaches a faulting predicate or load, the fault remains part of scalar behavior. Scalarization means encountering operations in scalar order, rather than introducing a fault from a moved access before the operations that should precede it.
How should we think about a predicate in the iteration where the loop exits?

The prefix selected for batching must be exit-free. Which accesses scalar execution performs in an exiting iteration depends on their actual order in that iteration; this hypothesis does not specify that order. It does not authorize batching an operation merely because it shares a lane with an exit test.
Does proving the scan and loads nonfaulting permit any access beyond the scalar exit?
No. An access beyond the scalar exit is forbidden even if it cannot fault. Exit-free reachability and nonfaulting access are distinct prerequisites; satisfying the latter does not remove the former.
If those proofs hold, can stores be committed in any order?

No. The requirement to preserve observable write ordering remains. The hypothesis addresses when predicate scans and loads may participate in a batched prefix without the specified store dependencies or early faults; it is not permission to reorder writes arbitrarily.
Can we treat this as an answer to the batching-proof question without asserting that the proofs have been constructed?

Yes. Path frequency does not tell you how much work each path performs or how long it takes. A successful guard may cover substantial or modest work, and checking the condition has its own cost.
